item.title: New AI Development Tools Integrate Security at Build and Runtime
item.description:
New AI Development Tools Integrate Security at Build and Runtime

As AI accelerates software development, hidden complexity has become a more critical security challenge. A new approach combining clean, curated base images, runtime profiling, and automated vulnerability remediation addresses this by reducing unnecessary code and exposure. Organizations continuously ingesting open source software must verify, trust, and evaluate components as they move through development, testing, and production following Zero Trust principles.

#AIsecurity #Containers #Vulnerabilities #CI/CD #ZeroTrust

Source: From Vulnerability Noise to Resilience: Rethinking Security in the AI Era

item.title: OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography
item.description:
OpenNHP toolkit hides infrastructure using zero-trust cryptography

OpenNHP is a lightweight, cryptography-powered, open-source toolkit implementing Zero Trust security for infrastructure, applications, and data. It serves as the reference implementation of the Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP) specification.

🔍 Overview

OpenNHP is designed to hide servers, ports, and domains from the public internet. In the AI era, visibility equates to vulnerability; OpenNHP inverts this model by remaining invisible until trusted. Consequently, scanners, bots, and AI-driven attackers find nothing to attack because nothing answers until a client proves its identity with a single encrypted packet.

🧩 How it works

The toolkit features two core protocols and a modular design inspired by the NIST Zero Trust Architecture:

  • Network-infrastructure Hiding Protocol (NHP): Conceals server ports, IP addresses, and domain names to protect applications and infrastructure from unauthorized access.
  • Data-content Hiding Protocol (DHP): Ensures data security and privacy via encryption and confidential computing, making data “usable but not visible.”

The architecture includes specific components that slot alongside existing IAM, DNS, FIDO, and Zero Trust policy engines:

Component Function
NHP-Agent Client that sends encrypted knock requests to gain access
NHP-Server Authenticates and authorizes requests; runs separately and is architecturally decoupled from the protected host
NHP-AC Access controller that manages firewall rules on the protected server
NHP-Relay HTTP-to-UDP bridge enabling browser-based agents to send NHP knocks via HTTPS
NHP-KGC Key Generation Center for Identity-Based Cryptography (IBC)

The workflow operates on a default-deny gate for every port, IP, and hostname:

  1. Registration (once per device): The agent generates its own key pair and enrolls the public key. The agent requests a one-time password (NHP_OTP), which the Server’s auth plugin delivers to the user (e.g., by email). The agent sends the OTP and its public key (NHP_REG), and the Server binds the key to the user and replies (NHP_RAK). The private key never leaves the device.
  2. Knock (every access): The agent sends an encrypted knock (NHP_KNK) to the Server. The Server validates the knock and sends an operation.

💡 Why it matters

Attackers can’t exploit what they can’t discover. NHP represents a next step in “hide the service first” designs, extending security stacks rather than forking them.

#OpenNHP #ZeroTrust #Cybersecurity #InfrastructureSecurity #OpenSource

Source: OpenNHP/opennhp

item.title: Tide Launches Raziel AI Security Tool Assuming Breach Imminence
item.description:
Tide Launches Raziel AI Security Tool Assuming Breach Imminence

Tide launched Raziel, an AI security tool designed under the assumption that hackers already exist within networks. This release addresses escalating risks from AI-generated code vulnerabilities and advanced attack models.

🔍 Overview

Tide’s Raziel operates on the principle that “hackers are inside”, acknowledging systemic flaws in traditional security paradigms. Co-founder Michael Loewy asserts the industry was losing ground to attackers even before AI, noting:

Before AI, a developer needed to be perfect all the time—perfectly patched, free of errors—while an attacker only needed one mistake to breach. It’s virtually impossible, which is why breaches are daily news. AI exacerbates this by enabling rapid production of error-prone code alongside sophisticated vulnerability exploitation.

🧩 How it works

Raziel implements emergent authority, where access permissions dynamically materialize only when identity, policy, context, and intent align—then dissolve. This replaces static credential storage with cryptographic fragmentation, ensuring no single point of failure exists. As Loewy states:

The problem is authority always lives somewhere, and someone always has access. We distribute it architecturally so nothing is inheritable.

⚙️ Key details

  • Raziel MCP Server: Named after the archangel of secrets, it educates AI agents on Tide’s authentication, threshold cryptography, and governance.
  • Blast Radius Mapping: Identifies post-breach risks like impersonation opportunities and unauthorized access pathways.
  • Verified Playbooks: Generates integration guides for self-hosted/managed deployments.
  • TideCloak Integration: Handles authentication/authorization via Tide’s Cybersecurity Fabric, keeping authority distributed.

🚀 Availability

Raziel launched Monday with open-source implementation via Tide’s GitHub. Resources include:

  • AI-generated white paper explaining emergent authority cryptography
  • TideCloak quickstart for greenfield projects

💡 Why it matters

Traditional security centralizes secrets—creating irresistible targets. Raziel’s model neutralizes this by making persistent authority impossible. Even with root access, attackers find nothing to inherit. As Loewy warns:

AI agents now create software and perform privileged actions. We must assume breaches will happen and architect accordingly.

#AISecurity #Cybersecurity #TideRaziel #EmergentAuthority #ZeroTrust #AIagents

Source: Tide launched Raziel for AI security. It assumes hackers are inside.
